issues.title: Use "site", not Origin
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
Privacy Pass made a serious error in using "origin" to describe the thing the tokens grant access to.  In practice, the privacy unit on the web is a [site](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#site).  That is, the set of web origins that share a registrable domain.

Because the website is something of a bystander in MoLE processing[^1], it's not a load-bearing notion, but I think that using "site" as the name of the primary beneficiary of the protocol is right.

[^1]: In practice the moderator is the one involved in the protocol interactions on behalf of each site.  The site really only has a few interactions: first, to identify a moderator; second, to receive the moderator's verdict about the client; and, third, to provide the moderator with feedback about interactions with the client.

issues.title: Should moderator identity be included in the nullifier
issues.author: ekr
issues.body: I've been reviewing the Longfellow mechanism (Section 4.2 of -protocol) and it seems like the nullifier just includes the epoch. As I've discussed with a few of you for Webbotauth, I think it's going to be desirable to sometimes use the same Endorsement with multiple Moderators, because we're leaning less on scarcity and more on the validation of the client. If I'm reading the description correctly, this will currently result in linkability. I think this can be readily addressed by including the identity of the Moderator in the computation of the nullifier, along with the epoch. Presumably we could have both Endorsements that allow this and forbid it, as desired.

comments.author: thibmeu
comments.body:
I think this is right for Longfellow.
Longfellow in [section 4.2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-jms-mole-protocols-00#name-longfellow) gives you a per epoch and global nullifier. I agree that we could derive a nullifier per moderator. This is probably desireable to support late binding of the endorsement to specific moderators.

However, that does not apply directly to IHAT, which requires the nullifier to be known at the time of endorsement. This implies that it cannot rely on the client knowing the moderator "identity" which is only known at the "Redeem & Issue" phase, possibly further down the line.

So to your suggestion
1. Longfellow could work in both modes,
2. IHAT would be restricted to a global nullifier and one-time use. Issuance and verification are orders of magnitude faster and smaller than with Longfellow, at the cost of more RTT and no late binding.

For IHAT, i'd double check with someone closer to the crypto work.

issues.title: Late Binding for TZ Endorsement
issues.author: cryptphil
issues.body:
It is possible to add late binding for the Tessaro and Zhu partial blind signature scheme such that the user can derive the nullifier for a specific moderator only during the endorsement redemption and must not decide on the redemption context already upfront during the endorsement issuance.

Concretely, during the Client Challenge phase, the Client samples one-time key `k`, computes its public value `K`, and puts K in the signed-message slot instead of Message(nf, ctx_red):
```
k = DeriveScalar(seeds[...], "k")
K = G.ScalarMultGen(k)
m = G.SerializeElement(K)
...
c = ComputeChallenge(ctx_iss, blinded_commitment, m)
```

During the Endorsement Redemption for a redemption context `ctx_red`, the Client derives the nullifier and proves its correctness:
```
R = CreateRedemptionBase(ctx_red)
nf = ScalarInverse(k) * R
pi_k = PoK{(k): K = G.ScalarMultGen(k) ∧ R = k * nf}
```

The Moderator recomputes `R` from `ctx_red`, verifies `pi_k` for `(K, nf, R)`, and checks the signature challenge over `m = SerializeElement(K)`, and whether `nf` is fresh.

**Note:** Endorsements remain single-show, each endorsement must only redeemed once as unlinkability is only guaranteed for one showing.

issues.title: Multishow IHAT
issues.author: cjpatton
issues.body:
Right now IHAT has roughly the following syntax:

* Issuance: `Client(ctx_red, ctx_iss, pkA) <--> Anchor(ctx_iss, skA)` That is, the client and anchor agree on the anchor's key and issuance context (client keeps the redemption context secret) and interact over some number of moves (2-3).
* Redemption: `Client(ctx_red, ctx_iss, anchor_set) <--> Moderator(ctx_red, ctx_iss, anchor_set)` Client and moderator agree on the issuance and redemption context and the anchor set. The client sends an endorsement covered by the anchor set.

Each IHAT token can be used just once. In some situations, it may be useful to instead be able to present the same token once (or perhaps multiple times) to many Moderators. Something like this:

* Issuance: `Client(ctx_iss, pkA) <--> Anchor(ctx_iss, skA)` Same as above, except `ctx_red` isn't determined until redemption time.
* Redemption: `Client(ctx_red, ctx_iss, anchor_set) <--> Moderator(ctx_red, ctx_iss, anchor_set)` Same as above. 

We know roughly how to do this with both Longfellow and Moussaka. In both cases, the solution involves adding an additional hash to the circuit that's used as a PRF applied to the redemption context (and perhaps presentation count, as in ARC). We can do the same thing for plain IHAT as well, but it would use the non-PQ-private trick in ARC.

I think EndorsementRequest and EndorsementResponse ought to have a field (following the token type) indicating the round round number. Otherwise we have to deal with this at the crypto layer, which somewhat complicates code design since we'd have to plumb the Anchor's protocol state through the protocol layer.

issues.title: Longfellow endorsement profile
issues.author: cryptphil
issues.body:
A few points in the Longfellow section (4.2) of MoLE protocols could be clarified:

- Replace “circuit” with “circuit artifact” or “circuits” as Longfellow uses two circuits packaged into one compressed artifact. So instead the circuit_id should identify this artifact, one could still keep `circuit_id` or rename it to `circuit_artifact_id`. The artifact specification containing the version, circuit IDs, and proof parameters should also be distributed out of band.

- Why is the Longfellow `Challenge` empty? One could also include a challenge digest into the Fiat-Shamir transcript, to explicitly bind the proof to the redemption (without making it a circuit public input).
- Should the credential expiry be considered? The Moderator could provide the currently accepted  `verification_time` in the Moderator configuration, which is used as a public circuit input to prove `validFrom <= verification_time <= validUntil`.
- The scarcity discussion may be a bit too broad and maybe needs some clarification. One might need Anchors to “participate in MoLE”, by adapting the issuance to allow for embedding commitment on a secret, which is provided by the Client, for deriving the nullifier. However, there might be existing credentials that already allow for the Client to embed a secret in some way; for instance in a nonce in OIDC (ref. [zk-login](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.11735)) or even in the seed for deriving the deviceKey in mdocs.

Once we publish the Longfellow MoLE prototype with the respective circuits under the cloudflare-research organization, we can also update the reference here.

Specify token issuance and redemption in enough detail to understand how the protocol works in broad strokes. Some details remain unspecified:

1. The wire format of messages sent in the protocol

2. The details of how the redemption proof is constructed. The circuit is described in a fair amount of detail, but it's not yet clear how the circuit is compiled into a proof. Also, an optimization that will be important in practice is to commit to intermediate states of the Keccak evaluation. We need to be precise about how this works.

Add estimates of the communication cost. An important observation (by Claude) is that the size of the redemption proof does not change that much as a function of the size of the Anchor Set. This is because most of the multiplications we're doing on the UOV maps depend on public constants rather than the witness, so these don't count towards the total proof size. We do have to commit to the selector vector, but this is tiny in comparison.

Update the constraints for the redemption proof. Claude came up with a set of "parity constraints" that appear to be a bit more robust. In particular the `b[i] * (b[i] - 1) = 0` checks don't actually prove that `b[i]` is `0` or `1` in a characteristic-2 field.

Minor things:

1. Zero-index vectors rather than start counting at 1. This is more consistent with Pythonic pseudocode, which we're approaching here.

Thanks @deep-inder! I mostly didn't follow the math, but left some comments mostly about presentation. On that I have two high level bits of feedback:

1. Stacked Sigmas is quite involved. I think the specification could use some sign posting to make it easier to digest. First, we should include a high level overview somewhere. Second, every once in a while we need to remind the reader of how the part they're reading relate to the bigger picture.

2. Not for this PR, but: I'm quite worried about the maintenance burden we're creating for ourselves. In the likely scenario that we need to make changes, it's going to be very difficult to propagate those changes correctly throughout the entire document. In the near future, I think we should transcribe the pseudocode here into a pure Python implementation that we can write tests for and generate test vectors from. We can then replace the psuedcode in the draft with Python snippets from the reference implementation. [This worked out really well for VDAF, which has a similar level of complexity](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-irtf-cfrg-vdaf-22.html#section-7.3.3). For what it's worth, this is something that Claude or GPT would be able to handle quite easily.
